titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The ladies look out over Valencia; King Yúsuf lands from Morocco (tiradas 87–90, lines 1610–1656)
part: Tiradas 87–90 · The ladies look out over Valencia; King Yúsuf lands from Morocco (lines 1610–1656)

sentences.t:
Adeliñó mio Çid con ellas al alcáç[e]r,
allá las subie en el más alto logar.
sentences.l:
Made-straight my Çid with them to-the alcáz[e]r,
there them he-was-taking-up in the most high place.
sentences.i: My Çid made straight for the citadel with them and took them up there to the highest place.
sentences.n: Tirada 87 (assonance á) — the ladies look out over Valencia from the citadel (Pidal: Las dueñas contemplan a Valencia desde el alcázar). The line-ends run alcáçer, logar, partes, çibdad, mar, grand: stressed á, with or without a following e. Adeliñó, preterite of adeliñar, 'to make straight for' (v. 1580). con ellas, Ximena and her daughters. The e of alcáç[e]r is Pidal's (in italics), as at v. 1571: alcáçer = alcázar, 'citadel'. subie, imperfect in -ie (= subía), 'he was taking them up', after the preterite: tense-mixing. logar = lugar.

sentences.t:
Ojos vellidos catan a todas partes,
miran Valençia cómmo yaze la çibdad,
e del otra parte a ojo han el mar,
sentences.l:
Eyes lovely look to all parts,
they-look-at Valençia how lies the city,
and from-the other side at eye they-have the sea,
sentences.i: Their lovely eyes gaze out on every side; they look at Valencia, how the city lies spread below, and on the other side they have the sea before their eyes;
sentences.n: Ojos vellidos, 'lovely eyes' (vellido = bellido, 'beautiful'): the ladies are named by their eyes. catan, catar, 'to look' (v. 2). miran Valençia cómmo yaze la çibdad, 'they look at Valencia, how the city lies': the thing seen is named first, then unfolded in a clause; yaze = yace. del otra parte = de la otra parte, el the old article form before a vowel, here with a feminine noun. a ojo han el mar, 'they have the sea in sight'; han, aver 'to have, hold'.

sentences.t:
miran la huerta, espessa es e grand,
e todas las otras cosas que eran de solaz;
alçan las manos pora Dios rogar,
desta ganançia cómmo es buena e grand.
sentences.l:
they-look-at the garden-plain, thick it-is and great,
and all the other things that were of delight;
they-raise the hands for God to-pray,
of-this gain how it-is good and great.
sentences.i: they look at the huerta, how dense and broad it is, and at all the other things that gave delight; and they raise their hands to pray to God for this gain, so good and so great.
sentences.n: huerta, the irrigated garden-plain round Valencia; espessa, 'thick, dense' with growth. Verse 1615b is printed wholly in italics in Pidal's edition: the whole line is his restoration. Unlike 1573b, it bears no number or letter in his margin and has no footnote; the label 1615b is ours, given after the preceding number by this edition's convention. solaz, 'pleasure, delight'. pora = para; pora Dios rogar, 'to pray God', the object before the infinitive. desta ganançia cómmo es buena e grand, 'for this gain, how good and great it is', the same unfolding construction as v. 1613; ganançia, 'gain, winnings'.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid e sus compañas tan a grand sabor están.
El ivierno es exido, que el março quiere entrar.
sentences.l:
My Çid and his companies so at great pleasure are.
The winter is gone-out, for the March wants to-enter.
sentences.i: My Çid and his companies are in such great delight. The winter is over, and March is about to come in.
sentences.n: tan a grand sabor, 'so much at great pleasure'; sabor, 'delight, liking'. compañas, 'companies, followers'. es exido, 'has gone out', exir (= salir) with ser as the auxiliary of a verb of motion. que, 'for'. quiere entrar, 'wants to come in', querer as 'to be about to': spring, the season of campaigns, is at hand.

sentences.t:
Dezir vos quiero nuevas de alle[n]t partes del mar,
de aquel rey Yúcef que en Marruecos está.
sentences.l:
To-tell to-you I-want news from beyo[n]d parts of-the sea,
of that king Yúcef who in Marruecos is.
sentences.i: Now I will tell you news from the lands beyond the sea, of that King Yúsuf who is in Morocco.
sentences.n: Dezir vos quiero, 'I want to tell you', the minstrel turning to his audience (compare v. 1603). nuevas, 'news, tidings'. alle[n]t = allende, 'beyond', the n Pidal's (in italics); alle[n]t partes del mar, 'the parts beyond the sea', North Africa. Pidal's note to v. 1621: Yúcef de Marruecos, the Almoravid emperor (introduction, pp. 27 and 17). The form Yúcef is kept in the interlinear; the translation gives Yúsuf. está, present, 'is', closing the tirada.

sentences.t:
Pesól al rey de Marruecos de mio Çid don Rodrigo:
“que en mis heredades fuertemie[n]tre es metido,
e él non gelo gradeçe sinon a Jesu Cristo.”
sentences.l:
It-weighed-on-him to-the king of Marruecos about my Çid don Rodrigo:
“that in my inherited-lands mightily he-is put,
and he not to-him-it gives-thanks except to Jesu Cristo.”
sentences.i: It weighed on the king of Morocco, the matter of my Çid Don Rodrigo: “He has thrust himself deep into my lands, and he gives thanks for it to none but Jesus Christ.”
sentences.n: Tirada 88 (assonance í-o) — the king of Morocco comes to besiege Valencia (Pidal: El rey de Marruecos viene a cercar a Valencia). The line-ends turn to Rodrigo, metido, Cristo, virtos, conplidos: stressed í, then o. Pesól = pesóle, 'it weighed on him', the le squeezed to -l and doubled by al rey. de, 'about'. heredades, 'lands held by inheritance': the king counts Valencia as his own. fuertemie[n]tre = fuertemente, the old adverb in -mientre, the n Pidal's (in italics). es metido, 'has thrust himself in', ser with the participle. gelo = ge (le) + lo, 'it to him'; ge looks forward to a Jesu Cristo; non … sinon, 'only': the Çid gives thanks for his gains to none but Christ.

sentences.t:
Aquel rey de Marruecos ajuntava sus virtos;
con çinquaenta vezes mill de armas, todos f[o]ron conplidos,
entraron sobre mar, en las barcas son metidos,
van buscar a Valençia a mio Çid don Rodrigo.
sentences.l:
That king of Marruecos was-gathering his forces;
with fifty times thousand of arms, all we[r]e furnished,
they-entered upon sea, in the boats they-are put,
they-go to-seek to Valençia to my Çid don Rodrigo.
sentences.i: That king of Morocco gathered his forces: fifty thousand men under arms, all fully equipped. They put out to sea, they are embarked in the boats, they go to Valencia to seek out my Çid Don Rodrigo.
sentences.n: ajuntava, 'was gathering' (ajuntar = juntar). virtos, most likely 'forces, hosts', as at v. 657, perhaps from Latin virtus, 'strength'; the exact sense is not certain. çinquaenta vezes mill, 'fifty times a thousand'; de armas, 'of arms', armed men. f[o]ron = fueron, the o Pidal's (in italics); conplidos, 'complete, fully furnished'. entraron sobre mar, 'they went upon the sea'. son metidos, 'are put (in)', present beside the preterites: tense-mixing. van buscar, ir + bare infinitive, 'they go to seek'; a Valençia … a mio Çid, the a of direction and the personal a side by side.

sentences.t: Arribado an las naves, fuera eran exidos.
sentences.l: Arrived have the ships, outside they-were gone-out.
sentences.i: The ships have come to land; the men have gone ashore.
sentences.n: Arribado an, 'have arrived', aver as the perfect auxiliary with naves as subject: arribar, 'to come to shore', is intransitive here, and with aver the participle agrees, if at all, only with an object, so it stays arribado. fuera eran exidos, 'they had gone out', ser + participle with a verb of motion, agreeing with the men understood; exir = salir. Here tirada 88 ends.

sentences.t:
Llegaron a Valençia, la que mio Çid a conquista,
fincaron las tiendas, e posan las yentes descreidas.
Estas nuevas a mio Çid eran venidas.
sentences.l:
They-arrived at Valençia, the-one that my Çid has conquered,
they-fixed the tents, and lodge the peoples unbelieving.
These news to my Çid were come.
sentences.i: They came to Valencia, the city my Çid has conquered; they pitched their tents, and the unbelieving hosts made camp. This news had reached my Çid.
sentences.n: Tirada 89 (assonance í-a) — three lines only, without a rubric in Pidal: conquista, descreidas, venidas, stressed í, then a. la que mio Çid a conquista, 'the one which my Çid has conquered': a = ha, and conquista is read as a short participle agreeing with la (Valencia), for conquistada, as conquistas = conquistadas at v. 1093 (todas conquistas las ha); the likelier reading, though the noun conquista is not ruled out. fincaron, fincar = hincar, 'to fix, pitch' (f- for h-). posan, 'they lodge, encamp', present after the preterite. yentes = gentes; descreidas, 'unbelieving'. eran venidas, 'had come', ser + participle agreeing with nuevas.

sentences.t:
“¡Grado al Criador e a[l] Padre espirital!
Todo el bien que yo he, todo lo tengo dela[n]t:
sentences.l:
“Thanks to-the Creator and to-[the] Father spiritual!
All the good that I have, all it I-hold befo[r]e:
sentences.i: “Thanks be to the Creator, the spiritual Father! All the good I have, I have it all here before me:
sentences.n: Tirada 90 (assonance á, with á-e) — the Çid's joy at the sight of the Moroccan hosts; Ximena's fear (Pidal: Alegría del Cid al ver las huestes de Marruecos. — Temor de Jimena). The line-ends mix á and á-e: espirital, delant, heredad, madre, fazen, salve. Pidal's note to v. 1633: the conjunction e is pleonastic, as at v. 300 (yo ruego a Dios e al Padre spirital), so the Creator and the spiritual Father are one: hence the translation. The l of a[l] is Pidal's (in italics). Grado, 'thanks'. espirital, here so spelt; spirital at v. 1651. he, aver 'to have'. dela[n]t = delante, 'before (me)', the n Pidal's (in italics): wife, daughters and city all in sight.

sentences.t:
con afán gané a Valençia, e ela por heredad,
a menos de muert no la puodo dexar;
sentences.l:
with toil I-won to Valençia, and her for inheritance,
short of death not her I-could leave;
sentences.i: with toil I won Valencia, and I hold her as my heritage; short of death I could not give her up.
sentences.n: afán, 'toil, hardship'. a Valençia, the personal a before the city's name. ela = ella, 'her', Valencia; e ela por heredad, '(I hold) her as heritage', the verb understood. a menos de muert, 'short of death, unless by dying'. puodo has the shape of a 3rd-singular preterite (= pudo), yet the Çid speaks of himself: 'I could not (would not be able to) leave her'; the form is odd, Pidal gives no note, and the exact reading is not certain.

sentences.t:
grado al Criador e a santa María madre,
mis fijas e mi mugier que las tengo acá.
sentences.l:
thanks to-the Creator and to holy Mary mother,
my daughters and my wife that them I-hold here.
sentences.i: thanks be to the Creator and to holy Mary, his mother: my daughters and my wife, I have them here with me.
sentences.n: santa María madre, 'holy Mary, mother (of God)', the stock phrase. que las tengo acá, 'that I have them here': either the relative que with the pronoun las repeating it, a common pattern, or que 'that' after grado (thanks … that I have them here), the nouns put first; the line allows both; tener, 'to have, hold'. acá, 'here'.

sentences.i: Delight has come to me from the lands beyond the sea; I shall take up arms, I cannot do otherwise; my daughters and my wife will see me fight;
sentences.n: Venídom = venido me, 'come to me', the me squeezed to -m; es venido, 'has come', ser with a verb of motion. deliçio, 'delight': the war that comes from Morocco is welcome to the Çid. Pidal's note sends to pp. 75–76 of his introduction, where (p. 77) he quotes this line: the Çid feels the fierce joy of the fight, and the battle offered him is 'a delicious gift brought from Africa'. d'allent = de allende, 'beyond'. entraré en las armas, 'I shall go into arms'; podré, future of poder. ve[e]rme an = me verán, the split future: the infinitive veer, the pronoun me, then an (= han); the second e is Pidal's (in italics), the old two-syllable veer. lidiar, 'to fight'.

sentences.t:
en estas tierras agenas verán las moradas cómmo se fazen,
afarto verán por los ojos cómmo se gana el pan.”
sentences.l:
in these lands foreign they-will-see the dwellings how themselves are-made,
fully they-will-see through the eyes how itself is-earned the bread.”
sentences.i: in these foreign lands they will see how homes are made; they will see their fill, with their own eyes, how bread is earned.”
sentences.n: agenas = ajenas, 'foreign, of others'. verán las moradas cómmo se fazen, 'they will see the dwellings, how they are made', with the noun named before the clause as at v. 1613; se fazen, the reflexive as passive; fazer = hacer (f- for h-). The sense of moradas is uncertain: 'dwellings', or 'how one dwells', how a home is held in a hostile land; the translation keeps the literal 'how homes are made'. afarto, 'fully, to the full' (a + harto, f- for h-). por los ojos, 'with (their own) eyes'. cómmo se gana el pan, 'how bread is earned': the Çid's living is won by the sword.

sentences.t:
Su mugier e sus fijas subiólas al alcáç[e]r,
alçavan los ojos, tiendas vi[di]eron finca[r]:
“¿Quês esto, Çid, sí el Criador vos salve!”
sentences.l:
His wife and his daughters he-took-them-up to-the alcáz[e]r,
they-were-raising the eyes, tents they-sa[w] to-be-fixe[d]:
“What-is this, Çid, so the Creator you save!”
sentences.i: He took his wife and daughters up into the citadel; they lifted their eyes and saw the tents being pitched. “What is this, Çid, so may the Creator save you?”
sentences.n: Su mugier e sus fijas subiólas, the objects named first and taken up again by -las: 'his wife and daughters, he took them up'. alcáç[e]r, as at v. 1610. vi[di]eron = vieron, the old preterite vidieron with di Pidal's (in italics); so too the r of finca[r]; the line is partly his restoration. tiendas … fincar, 'tents being pitched'. Pidal's note to v. 1644: in Florence de Rome (a French chanson of the early thirteenth century, vv. 1059–80), Florence too looks from a window, sees the army drawn up, and in fear would avoid the battle, but her father reassures her. Quês = qué es. sí el Criador vos salve, 'so may the Creator save you', sí = así, the oath of entreaty.

sentences.t:
—“Ya mugier ondrada, non ayades pesar!
Riqueza es que nos acreçe maravillosa e grand:
sentences.l:
—“O wife honored, not you-may-have sorrow!
Wealth it-is that to-us increases marvellous and great:
sentences.i: “Ah, honoured wife, do not be troubled! It is riches coming to us, marvellous and great:
sentences.n: Ya, 'O!', the vocative particle (Arabic yā). ondrada = honrada. non ayades pesar, 'do not have sorrow': ayades, present subjunctive of aver, makes the polite negative command. pesar, 'grief, distress'. Riqueza es, 'it is wealth', the Moorish host seen as plunder to come. acreçe, 'grows, increases (for us)', acreçer; maravillosa e grand agree with riqueza.

sentences.t:
a poco que viniestes, presend vos quieren dar:
por casar son vuestras fijas, adúzenvos axuvar.”
sentences.l:
at little that you-came, present to-you they-want to-give:
for to-marry are your daughters, they-bring-you trousseau.”
sentences.i: you have scarcely come, and they want to give you a present: your daughters are yet to be married, and they bring you a trousseau for them.”
sentences.n: a poco que viniestes, 'a little after you came, scarcely had you come'; viniestes, 2nd plural preterite, the plural of respect. presend = presente, 'a present'. por casar son, 'are yet to be married'. adúzenvos = os aducen, 'they bring you' (aduzir, 'to bring'). Pidal's note to v. 1650: 'they bring you the ajuar', the household goods for the marriage; on axuvar he sends to v. 2571. The Çid jests: the spoil of the Moroccan host will furnish his daughters' weddings. axuvar = ajuar (x = sh); Pidal's gloss is followed, and the jest rests on it.

sentences.t: —“A vos grado, Çid, e al Padre spirital.”
sentences.l: —“To you thanks, Çid, and to-the Father spiritual.”
sentences.i: “Thanks be to you, Çid, and to the spiritual Father.”
sentences.n: Ximena's answer, one line. A vos grado, 'thanks to you', the vos of respect. Padre spirital, 'the spiritual Father', as at v. 300 and, spelt espirital, at v. 1633.

sentences.t:
—“Mugier, se[e]d en este palaçio, en el alcáç[e]r;
non ayades pavor por que me veades lidiar,
sentences.l:
—“Wife, st[a]y in this palace, in the alcáz[e]r;
not you-may-have fear because me you-may-see fight,
sentences.i: “Wife, stay here in this palace, in the citadel; have no fear at seeing me fight,
sentences.n: se[e]d, imperative of seer, 'to sit, stay, be', the second e Pidal's (in italics). palaçio, 'palace, hall'; en el alcáç[e]r, the same place named again, the e Pidal's as before. non ayades pavor, the polite negative command, as v. 1647; pavor, 'fear'. por que me veades lidiar, 'because you see me fight', veades the present subjunctive of veer.

sentences.i: by the grace of God and of holy Mary his mother, my heart grows great because you are here before me; with God, this battle I am bound to win.”
sentences.n: merced, 'grace, favour'. créçem = créceme, 'grows (in) me', the me squeezed to -m: 'my heart swells'. Pidal's note to v. 1655 sends to p. 93, n. 2, of his introduction for créçem el coraçón; in this printing p. 93 has no footnote, but on p. 77 he quotes vv. 1653–55: the presence of the ladies increases the Çid's courage. estades = estáis; delant = delante, 'in front, present'. aquesta = esta. la he de arrancar, 'I have to win it': aver de + infinitive, of what must and will happen, with the pronoun la repeating aquesta lid. arrancar, 'to rout, win the field' (compare arrancada, v. 1573b). Here tirada 90 ends.
